excerpt: How four American executives went from governing a civilian prison camp in Manila to an unmarked grave in Malate—and how the Army found them.
dek: Inside the arrest, disappearance, and discovery of four expats in wartime Manila.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
imageAlt: The July 12, 1942 front page of The Sunday Tribune displays above the fold a photograph of the internees relaxing on the University of Santo Tomas campus grounds.
bodyText:
While on Saipan preparing for the 70th anniversary of the battle, I came across a photograph of a 1942 front page from *The Sunday Tribune*. Printed entirely above the fold was a large image of people appearing to relax on the grass of a public park.

Looking closer, I recognized the building behind them: the main building of the University of Santo Tomas in Manila.Founded in 1611, twenty-five years before Harvard, it was the institution where generations of Philippine lawmakers,justices, and presidents were educated.

What looked like a lazy afternoon in the park was the opening chapter of a four-year internment. The lawn was broad,the shadow of the main building long and familiar, but the people sitting on the grass were not parkgoers. They were foreign civilians brought to the campus by Japanese forces to establish the largest internment camp in the Philippines.

That photograph started a search for details. Several thousand American and British expats spent nearly four years behind those walls before their liberation in February 1945. Four internee leaders were taken from their quarters one night near the end of the war and never returned. Among them was Carroll C. Grinnell, General Electric's vice president for the Far East.

#### The Line at Santo Tomas

Before the war, Grinnell managed business operations in Manila. When Japanese forces occupied the city in 1942 and converted the university into a camp, the internees formed a self-governing committee and chose Grinnell as chairman.

For thirty-seven months, he directed daily operations inside the camp. He arranged for medicine, clothing, and food,signing personal checks backed by General Electric to buy provisions from local vendors on credit. His job required maintaining order among the captives while dealing directly with Japanese authorities—a position that left him exposed to suspicion from both sides.

On January 15, 1945, less than three weeks before American troops reached the camp, Grinnell vanished. Three other internee leaders disappeared with him: Alfred Francis Duggleby, Clifford Lawrence Larsen, and Ernest Emil Johnson.The Kempeitai, the Japanese military police, had taken them during the night.

#### Tracing the Missing

After Santo Tomas was liberated on February 3, 1945, Army investigators began looking for the four men.

A tip led searchers to Dr. Antonio Sison, director of the Philippine General Hospital, who had been held by Japanese police in late December. Sison remembered seeing Johnson in custody, pointing investigators toward the residence of Dr. Baldomero Roxas in Malate.

![Dr. Baldomero Roxas' residence](/assets/uploads/cms/dr-baldomero-roxas-house.jpg "The house of Dr. Baldomero Roxas, where a witness (Dr. Sison) saw Ernest Emil Johnson, had been in the custody of the Kempeitai.")

Initial searches of the property turned up nothing. Subsequent digs on the grounds uncovered unmarked graves.

Grinnell’s body was identified by his clothing: khaki trousers and a cream-colored Viyella shirt marked with the initials *CCG*. Near him lay the remains of Duggleby, Larsen, and Johnson. All four had been bound and executed, suspected of sending information outside the walls.

Dr. T.D. Stevenson examined the remains on February 22, 1945, noting that precise medical identification was impossible due to decomposition. That afternoon, the four men were buried near the east corner of the Seminary Building on the campus grounds.

#### Records and Accounts

Statements from former internees document Grinnell's actions inside the camp.

Neville Stopford, interned as a child, recalled the situation the committee faced: "These men held a grave responsibility. They had to walk a fine line... They were discovered, hands bound and beheaded—a tragic end for those who had worked tirelessly for us."

Internee Eleanor Garen stated that Grinnell's emergency food purchases kept her alive through the worst shortages.After returning to the United States, she contacted General Electric to pay back the cost of the food she received.

When Ruth Grinnell later accepted the Medal of Freedom for her husband, it marked the official end of a search that began with four missing men and ended in a shallow grave in Malate. What remains of Carroll Grinnell is recorded in declassified Army reports, old newspaper photos, and the receipts of people who survived because he was there.

Looking back on the university's long history, the four-year internment remains a bitter chapter. Were it not for the sudden arrival of the U.S. Army, orders to execute the remaining internees would have been carried out on the campus grounds. The swift and decisive actions of guerrilla intelligence and the U.S. Army 1st Cavalry Division spared the internees from wholesale carnage, ultimately saving thousands from a brutal end. Grinnell and three others were not as fortunate.
